text: LATIN TIMES: Natanael Cano Sings to Los Salazar: New Album Revives Narco Ballads Despite Crackdown August 31, 2026 | 🟡 📰 Latin Times frames Cano's new album as "reviving narco ballads" in defiance of a crackdown — one track name-checks Los Salazar, a Sinaloa-linked group. 🔍 What it soft-pedals: the "crackdown" is real state policy, with promoters submitting set lists to authorities for approval. 🇲🇽 Several Mexican states now bar songs glorifying organized crime — an artistic-freedom fight the piece flattens into outlaw cool. • Promoters submit set lists; authorities decide "which songs he cannot perform" • 15-track "Vol. 1" released Aug 28, invoking Los Salazar Source

NY POST: Made in Mexico $9K EV could be a California commuter's dream August 27, 2026 | 🟡 📰 A $9K homegrown Mexican EV — and the Post's angle is "Chinese tech" in the URL and golf-cart mockery in the copy. 🔍 The Olinia is openly a 31-mph city car for short urban trips, judged here by whether it can do 70 on the 405. 🇲🇽 State-backed, Mexican-designed, built for local commutes and deliveries — measured against a highway it was never meant for. • "These aren't exactly built for cruising down the 405 at 70 mph" • Headline sells it; the URL slugs it "with Chinese tech" Source

REUTERS: New foreign investment in Mexico stalls as companies fret over USMCA uncertainty September 1, 2026 | 🟡 📰 The lede is investment "stalling" — then the copy admits total FDI hit a RECORD ~$35B in H1 2026. New/greenfield spending fell, so the headline picks the gloomy half. 🔍 The named culprit is Washington: Trump declined to renew USMCA, opting for annual reviews. 🇲🇽 The "uncertainty" spooking investors is US-manufactured — yet the frame lands on Mexico as the risky bet, not on the country tearing up the treaty. • "reconsidering their investment plans… relocate to Asia" • Washington "declined to renew it, instead opting for annual reviews" Source

REUTERS: Bomb attacks by Mexican gangs on the rise, officials say September 1, 2026 | 🟡 📰 A car bomb outside a police HQ in Ojocaliente, Zacatecas injured 11 and damaged ~40 buildings — retaliation for an arrest, officials say. 🔍 Reuters ran the numbers straight: 1 such attack in 2024, 6 in 2025, 10 so far in 2026. 🇲🇽 The escalation is real but geographic — Zacatecas and Michoacán — not the whole country. Data-driven wire copy, credited to Gov. David Monreal on the record. • "an evolution in the operations of criminal groups" • Zacatecas bombings: 1 (2024) → 6 (2025) → 10 (2026) Source

NYT: "The Nest of Snakes": Warring Cartels Target Women in Mexico August 31, 2026 | 🔴 📰 The NYT gives Sinaloa's two-year internal war a horror-movie title — "The Nest of Snakes" — and makes murdered women the narrative hook. 🔍 The real story is a fragmented cartel civil war concentrated in a few states, not a nationwide collapse. 🇲🇽 Left out: Mexico's national homicides fell ~51% in July to a 12-year low. The bloodletting is localized — and it's between factions the US kingpin strategy helped splinter. • Loaded framing: "The Nest of Snakes" • A two-year Sinaloa faction war, not a countrywide surge Source

🇲🇽🏭 <u>MEXICO EXPORTS LIKE NEVER BEFORE — RECORD $81.4B IN JULY</u>

Trump's tariffs were meant to break Mexico. Instead exports hit an all-time monthly record of $81.42 billion in July — up 43.7% year-on-year, INEGI reports — with the United States still the top destination by far. Even in the middle of a tariff war, Mexico closed the January–July period with a $9.26 billion trade surplus.

✊🇲🇽 <u>MEXICO CITY EXPANDS ITS UNIVERSAL BASIC INCOME</u>

Clara Brugada handed out 20,000 new grants under Mexico City's Universal Citizen Income — 2,000 pesos every two months for residents aged 57-59, now reaching 107,000 people and headed to 150,000 this year. "Redistributing income isn't giving you a handout — it's returning part of the wealth you produced," Brugada said. The capital is piloting what could become a lifelong guaranteed income, a first in Mexico.

🕊️🇲🇽 <u>MEXICO CITY MOVES TO LEGALIZE EUTHANASIA — 86% BACK IT</u>

Days after the capital's first-ever march for the right to a dignified death, a survey found 86% of Mexico City residents support legalizing euthanasia. Mayor Clara Brugada came out in favor of advancing the debate, and the "Ley Trasciende" initiative — "my life, my death, my decision" — now heads toward consultation with affected families, doctors and specialists. A humanist reform grounded in personal autonomy.

📱🇲🇽 <u>81% OF MEXICO'S TEACHERS BACK REGULATING PHONES IN CLASS</u>

Mexico consulted 565,396 teachers — one of the largest such exercises ever — and 81% backed clear rules for phones and screens in schools, with 48% reporting cellphones wreck students' attention. "Social networks generate messages of hate and abuse that children wouldn't otherwise encounter," Sheinbaum said, as the SEP drafts national guidelines built from teachers' own voices rather than a top-down ban.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>MEXICAN FAMILIES DROWNING IN BANK DEBT AT RECORD RATES</u>

Household loan defaults just hit an all-time high — Banco de México reports overdue consumer credit reached 64.5 billion pesos, up 32.8% in real terms in a single year, with credit-card delinquency alone soaring 53%. This is the inheritance of a neoliberal banking system run by foreign megabanks charging usurious rates — precisely the model the 4T's Banco del Bienestar was built to break.
